opus-5.5.text:
The key difference, for me, is interactivity, and more specifically, action conditioning.

Veo is a video generation model. You give it a prompt, maybe an image, and it produces a clip. It's incredibly good at visual quality and at capturing a lot of physics implicitly. But once generation starts, you're watching a movie. You can't step in and say, "Now I turn left," or "Now I push this object," and have the model respond to that in the moment.

Genie is built around exactly that. At every step it takes the current state of the world plus an action from the agent or the user, and predicts what happens next. That's the textbook definition of a world model: a transition function from state and action to the next state. If you come from robotics or reinforcement learning like I do, that's the thing you really want, because it's what lets you plan, simulate counterfactuals, and train policies inside the model.

Two other things follow from that. First, consistency over time. If I walk away from a room in Genie and come back, the room should still be there, looking the same. A video model only needs to look plausible for a few seconds, but a world model has to keep a persistent world as you interact with it over longer horizons. Second, real-time responsiveness. To be interactive, it has to generate frame by frame fast enough that a person or an agent can act in the loop, which is a very different engineering target from producing a beautiful eight-second clip offline.

That said, I don't see them as opposites. Veo shows how much knowledge about the world you can absorb just by learning from huge amounts of video. You could even say Veo has a world model inside it. Genie takes that understanding and makes it controllable. For robotics, controllability is what matters, because a robot doesn't just watch the world, it acts on it and needs to know what happens when it does.

r001.rationale: The response says Genie takes an action from the user or agent at every step and predicts what happens next, while Veo does not let users intervene once generation starts.

fable-5.1.text:
The key difference is interactivity. Veo takes a prompt and generates a fixed video clip. You describe a scene, it renders it, and that's it. It's essentially predicting pixels forward in time without anyone being able to intervene. Genie is different because at every step, it takes an action as input. You press a button, the model has to figure out what happens next given that action. That's what a world model really is from a robotics or reinforcement learning point of view: a simulator you can act in, not a movie you watch.

That matters a lot for people like me working on robots. For training a robot, I don't just need to know what the world looks like, I need to know how it responds when the robot does something. If I push the cup, does it slide, does it tip over? A video generator can produce a very beautiful clip of a cup, but it doesn't have to be consistent with my choices. Genie has to learn that causal structure, because the action is part of the conditioning. So it's learning something closer to physics and dynamics, even if it's still imperfect.

The other piece is consistency over time. In a game-like setting, you might turn left, look around, turn back, and the world should still be there. Genie has to maintain state in a way that is testable, because the user can go back and check. With Veo, nobody is testing it that way. So I think of Veo as a very strong content generation model, and Genie as a first real attempt at an interactive environment, which is the thing you would eventually want to train agents inside of.

r001.rationale: The response says Genie takes an action at every step and uses it to determine what happens next, contrasting this with Veo’s fixed video clip. This clearly identifies users’ actions as changing the generated sequence.

astra-6.text:
For me, the key distinction is interaction. Veo generates a video: you give it a prompt, and it produces a sequence of frames. Genie is closer to a world model because you can take an action, and the environment responds. What happens next depends on what you do.

That matters for an agent. To plan, you want to ask, “If I take this action, what will happen? What if I take a different action?” A world model lets you explore those possibilities. So I wouldn’t say video generation and world modeling are completely separate—generating convincing video requires some understanding of how the world works. But Genie’s action-conditioned, interactive nature makes it closer to the kind of world model an agent can use.

r001.rationale: The response says Genie is interactive: users can take actions, and what happens next depends on those actions. It gives this as the reason Genie is closer to a world model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is interaction. Veo generates a video from a prompt, but Genie lets an agent take an action and see how the world responds. That action-conditioned prediction is much closer to what we mean by a world model.

For example, if I move left, what will I see next? If I interact with an object, how will the scene change? You need to be able to keep asking those questions as you act. A video can look very realistic, but realism alone doesn’t make it a world model. The important thing is whether it can model the consequences of your actions.

r001.rationale: The response says Genie lets an agent act and see how the world responds, including how moving or interacting changes what comes next. It identifies this action-conditioned prediction as why Genie is closer to a world model.
